messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Extracting subgraph based on vertex attribute or restrict calculation of node level indices
messages.body_plain:
To calculate degree over a subset of nodes, use the "nodes" option for the degree function. For example, to calculate outdegree (supposing your network is directed) for males only, you'd have something like:

degree(YourNetwork, nodes=(YourNetwork%v%"Gender"=="m"), cmode="outdegree")

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Number of isolates in a network
messages.body_plain:
If I'm not mistaken, it's just a matter of using the following if
'foo' is a network object:
length(isolates(foo))
isolates(foo) returns a vector of the isolate nodes and you want the length.

Ben

messages.body_plain:

plot by hand using the "interactive" argument.  Make sure to save the

mycoords <- plot(mynetwork, interactive=TRUE)
# followed by:
plot(mynetwork, coord=mycoords)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] plot network layout
messages.body_plain:
You might have better luck using "fruchtermanreingold" instead and  
increasing layout.par$repulse.rad until the network spreads out more:

layout.par <- list(repulse.rad=<some large number>)

Then

plot(mynetwork,layout.par=layout.par)

Iterate until you get something that looks good.

Keep in mind that if your network is sufficiently large and dense,  
it's always going to look "packed together" on a graph.

-AHM

Where it's relatively simple to calculate the assortativity  
coefficient (based on the mixingmatrix values), as introduced by  
Newman, with statnet, it will be difficult to write a function to  
determine the standard deviation for that value.

So I thought I'm asking the community before I try to create such a  
function. Does anybody have an approach or even better a function to  
calculate this value?

Many thanks ...
rico

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Research Associate in Network Epidemiology using Bipartite Networks at the University of Cambridge
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet List,

Sorry if this is off-topic, but I'm looking for a networky person for 
the following position. Simulation/ERGM experience (especially on 
bipartite networks) would be great!

UNIVERSITY OF CAMBRIDGE

DEPARTMENT OF VETERINARY MEDICINE

Research Associate in Network Epidemiology using Bipartite Networks

Stipend 7 ?27,183.00 to ?35,469.00

Limit of Tenure: 31 August 2010, with reappointment on a yearly basis 
until 31 August 2011.
 
Venues, such as bars and clubs, can shape social, sexual, and drug-use 
networks. This project involves the development of statistical, 
computational, and mathematical models of social networks and disease 
transmission, which will be applied to a dataset of HIV risk behaviours 
and drug use collected from men who have sex with men in bars and clubs 
in San Diego, California. Simulation models will be used to generate 
bipartite networks, representing the relationship between individuals 
and the places they visit. This project will guide further data 
collection from cities in the United Kingdom. Models of how individuals 
choose where to go, and how they behave there, can also be adapted to 
other systems, such as how different host species are infected by 
different pathogen species.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM null model with fixed degree distribution
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ERGM null model with fixed degree distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In the last few days I tried to find an access to the world of the  
ERGM's. But for people which are not that familiar with statistics,  
like me, this seems to be rather difficult. The information in all the  
articles is just overwhelming.

So, I thought you could maybe give me some help with a particular  
question I would like to answer by the use of the ergm package.

I try to study the assortative mixing, based on the gender, in the  
network. There is some good and clear advise in the "statnet Tutorial"  
article on how to do this. But in the tutorial they use, as I  
understand it, an Erd?s-R?nyi Model as the null model. For my network,  
however, it seems to be better to use a network with a fixed degree  
distribution as the null model. Is it convenient to get such a model  
with the following command:

R> mod_deg <- ergm(net_orig ~ degree(unique(degree(net_orig,  
gmode="graph"))))

Based on the model, I would like to study the assortative mixing by  
gender:

R> mod_deg_sex <- ergm(net_orig ~ degree(unique(degree(net_orig,  
gmode="graph"))) + nodemix("SEX"))

[...]

mix.SEX.f.f  -1.0693    14.7238        NA   0.942
mix.SEX.f.m  -1.0430    16.1148        NA   0.948
mix.SEX.m.m  -0.9059    11.3241        NA   0.936
mix.SEX.f.u  -1.4389     5.1658        NA   0.781
mix.SEX.m.u  -1.2306     4.8916        NA   0.801
mix.SEX.u.u     -Inf         NA        NA      NA

[...]

R> mod_deg_sex$mle.lik
[1] -692.3349

(u stands for nodes for which the gender is unknown)

Does this output mean, that the assortative mixing  by gender is  
(statistically) not a factor which leads to the given network  
structure (high std. errors, and p-values)?

Any help and comments are highly appreciated.

Thank you
rico

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rico.  Just a quick response for now:

Adding degree terms to an ergm won't fix the degree distribution.  To  
do that you should use the "constraints" option with the ergm  
function.  In the help file for the ergm function, check out the  
specific section that discusses "constraints" and see if that makes  
sense.

Sorry for the brief reply!
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM, missing data, and dyadcov and edgecov terms
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ERGM, missing data, and dyadcov and edgecov terms
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a Statnet-ERGM question that I suspect has been asked and  
answered, but so far my search of the archives has not yielded an  
answer.

I am working with a directed graph. A small number of actors in my  
population have missing data for their edges.  However, I have a rich  
set of attribute data for these actors, which leads me to retain dyads  
in which they are alters for models w/ nodematch terms, etc.

Certain ERGM terms (e.g., edgecov) require that the dataset analyzed  
consist of all possible edges in the data along with values for  
whatever edge covariates are of interest.  In my case, given missing  
data, all possible edges (possible = possibly observed) would not be a  
square matrix, because only actors with alter data can be egos, while  
all actors can be alters.

I assume the edgecov term expects a square matrix anyway.  If so, I  
seem to have two options:

1) Reduce my data to only edges in which ego and alter both are  
complete in terms of tie data.
2) Provide ERGM with the full square matrix, including edges that I  
can't observe.

If #2, to the extent I have a node attribute indicating whether the  
node's edges were missing rather than null, are there additional  
statements that can be made to capture that only certain directed  
edges can be observed?

As a reminder (from the JOSS ERGM article):

"The x argument is either a square matrix of covariates, one for each  
possible edge in the network, covariates, or a network; if the latter,  
optional argument attrname provides the name of the quantitative edge  
attribute to use for covariate values (in this case, missing edges in  
x are assigned a covariate value of zero). "

It appears to call for the square matrix, but that doesn't feel quite  
right.

Any suggestions, best practices, readings, or considerations are  
appreciated....

Thanks!

Matthew
